lessonTitle: Auscultation and Completing the Abdominal Examination

blocks.text: A man with three days of colicky abdominal pain and vomiting lies still on the couch. You place your stethoscope on his abdomen and hear high-pitched, tinkling, rushing sounds that come in waves. Those few seconds of listening, followed by a check of his groins, can point you toward bowel obstruction and the hernia that may be causing it.

blocks.markdown: In the abdominal examination the usual order is **inspection, palpation, percussion, then auscultation**. The order differs from the rest of the body because palpation and percussion can alter bowel activity, so listening is traditionally done **after** the hands-on phases in many teaching schemes, although some schools listen before deep palpation. Whichever order your school uses, the content is the same. Auscultation asks two questions: *is the bowel making sounds, and what kind?* and *is blood flow through the abdominal arteries turbulent?*. After auscultation you **complete** the examination by checking the hernial orifices and by deciding which further examinations belong in a full abdominal assessment.

blocks.title: Bowel sounds and bruits
blocks.text: **Bowel sounds** are gurgling noises produced by the movement of gas and fluid through the lumen during peristalsis. A **bruit** is a whooshing sound heard over an artery when blood flow is turbulent, usually because the lumen is narrowed or dilated.

blocks.markdown:
### Technique for bowel sounds

1. Warm the diaphragm of the stethoscope and rest it lightly on the abdomen.
2. Listen in one place, classically just below and to the right of the umbilicus (over the region of the ileocaecal valve), because bowel sounds are transmitted widely through the abdomen.
3. Listen long enough before judging: bowel sounds are intermittent, so a conclusion of *absent* should not be drawn until you have listened for about **two minutes** (teaching texts quote one to two minutes; use the full period before calling sounds absent).
4. Describe what you hear as **normal**, **increased** (hyperactive), **reduced**, or **absent**, and note the character (for example tinkling).

blocks.caption: Patterns of bowel sounds and what they suggest
rows: Intermittent soft gurgles every few seconds to minutes
Loud, high-pitched, rushing sounds in waves, often with colicky pain
Mechanical obstruction proximal to the block (early); also gastroenteritis
Silence after a full listening period
Paralytic (adynamic) ileus, advanced obstruction, generalised peritonitis

blocks.title: Interpreting what you hear
blocks.prompt: A 70-year-old woman, two days after a hip replacement, has a distended, soft, non-tender abdomen and has vomited twice. You listen over the right iliac fossa for two full minutes and hear no bowel sounds. What is your interpretation and what do you do next?

steps.text: State the finding precisely: no bowel sounds after a full two-minute listening period at one site, so the finding is genuinely absent rather than simply not yet heard.
Link the finding to mechanism: peristalsis has stopped. After surgery, opioid analgesia and immobility commonly cause paralytic ileus, in which the bowel is not obstructed but is not contracting.
Look for supporting signs: distension with a soft non-tender abdomen fits ileus. Guarding or rigidity would instead suggest peritonitis.
Act on it: report the finding to a senior colleague, and recognise that absent bowel sounds alone are not a diagnosis but are part of the overall picture.

blocks.answer: Absent bowel sounds with distension and vomiting in this context suggest paralytic ileus; the finding is reported and interpreted together with palpation findings.

blocks.markdown:
### Listening for bruits

Place the diaphragm over the **epigastrium in the midline** to listen for an **aortic bruit**, and just above the umbilicus on each side of the midline, over the **renal arteries**. A bruit in the epigastrium may suggest aortic narrowing or an aneurysm; a renal artery bruit may suggest renal artery stenosis, in a patient with hypertension. A **hepatic bruit** (heard over the liver) is uncommon but can occur with hepatocellular carcinoma or alcoholic hepatitis. A bruit is a clue, not a diagnosis, and always needs correlation with the history and the rest of the examination.

blocks.title: Listen before you declare silence
blocks.text: Bowel sounds are intermittent. Calling them absent after a few seconds is a common mistake. Listen for about two minutes at one site before recording the sounds as absent.

blocks.markdown:
### Examining the hernial orifices

A **hernia** is protrusion of a viscus or part of one through a defect in the wall that normally contains it. In the groin the sites to examine are the **inguinal** and **femoral** canals. Both sides are always checked, and the patient is examined **standing**, because gravity and raised intra-abdominal pressure make a hernia more obvious than when lying down.

- Expose from the umbilicus to the mid-thigh with consent, privacy and a chaperone if the examiner and patient wish.
- **Inspect** the groins and scrotum for a swelling at rest.
- Ask the patient to **cough** (or strain) and watch for a bulge: this is a **cough impulse**.
- Identify the **pubic tubercle** (the bony point at the medial end of the inguinal ligament). An **inguinal hernia** emerges **above and medial** to the pubic tubercle. A **femoral hernia** emerges **below and lateral** to it.
- Ask whether the swelling can be gently pushed back (**reducible**). Never force an irreducible, tender swelling.

blocks.caption: Inguinal versus femoral hernia on examination
rows: Often present but may be small
Lower in indirect/direct types, but present
Higher because the neck is narrow

blocks.title: Placing a groin swelling
blocks.prompt: A 55-year-old man standing before you has a lump in the right groin that appears on coughing and disappears when he lies down. You palpate the pubic tubercle and find the lump's neck lies just above and medial to it. What is the most likely diagnosis, and what is your next step?

steps.text: Reducibility on lying down together with a cough impulse suggests a hernia rather than a lymph node or an abscess.
Use the landmark: the pubic tubercle is the reference point. A neck above and medial to the tubercle places the hernia through the inguinal canal, so it is an inguinal hernia.
Check the other side and examine the scrotum, because inguinal hernias may extend into it.
Record whether it is reducible and tender, and report any irreducible painful lump urgently.

blocks.answer: A right inguinal hernia; examine the other groin and scrotum and document reducibility and tenderness.

items: Examine the external genitalia (scrotum, testes, penis in male patients) as part of a complete assessment, with consent.
Perform a digital rectal examination when clinically indicated, with consent and a chaperone, and inspect the glove for stool colour and blood.
Examine for lymph nodes in the groins and the left supraclavicular fossa when the picture warrants it.
Check for ankle and sacral oedema, and examine the other systems (cardiovascular and respiratory) as indicated.
Test the urine with a dipstick and record the full set of vital signs.

blocks.title: Consent and chaperone
blocks.text: Genital and rectal examination require explicit consent, a clear explanation, and a chaperone offered in line with local policy. If the patient declines, accept the refusal and document it.

points: Listen for about two minutes at one site before calling bowel sounds absent; tinkling hyperactive sounds suggest obstruction, silence suggests ileus or peritonitis.
Listen for bruits over the aorta and renal arteries, and over the liver if indicated; a bruit is a clue that needs clinical correlation.
Examine both groins with the patient standing and coughing; inguinal hernias lie above and medial to the pubic tubercle, femoral hernias below and lateral.
Complete the examination with genitalia, a digital rectal examination when indicated, lymph nodes, oedema, urinalysis and vital signs.

questions.stem: How long should you listen at one site before recording bowel sounds as absent?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: bowel sounds are intermittent so a long listening period is needed.
distractorRationale.b: Far too short; intermittent sounds would be missed.
distractorRationale.c: Still too short for a conclusion of absence.
distractorRationale.d: Coughing is used for hernias, not for judging bowel sounds.

questions.explanation: Bowel sounds occur intermittently, not continuously. A listening period of about two minutes avoids wrongly diagnosing ileus or peritonitis from a brief silence.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man has colicky central abdominal pain, vomiting and no flatus for two days. On auscultation you hear frequent, loud, high-pitched tinkling sounds in rushes. These findings are most consistent with:

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the bowel contracts forcefully against a blockage, giving loud tinkling sounds with colic.
distractorRationale.b: Ileus gives reduced or absent sounds, not hyperactive ones.
distractorRationale.c: Normal sounds are soft and intermittent, and would not accompany this presentation.
distractorRationale.d: A bruit is a whoosh over an artery, not tinkling bowel noise.

questions.explanation: Hyperactive tinkling sounds in rushes with colic, vomiting and absolute constipation reflect peristalsis working against a blockage. In paralytic ileus the bowel is silent because peristalsis has stopped.

questions.stem: Where do you place the stethoscope to listen for an aortic bruit?

options.text: In the midline of the epigastrium
Over the right iliac fossa only

questions.correctOptionText: In the midline of the epigastrium

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the abdominal aorta lies in the midline above the umbilicus.
distractorRationale.b: This is the usual site for bowel sounds, not an aortic bruit.
distractorRationale.c: The aorta has already bifurcated by this level.
distractorRationale.d: This is a lymph node site, not an auscultation site for aortic flow.

questions.explanation: The abdominal aorta runs in the midline, so an aortic bruit is sought over the epigastrium. Renal artery bruits are sought slightly above the umbilicus to either side of the midline.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man stands in front of you with a groin lump that appears on coughing. The neck of the lump lies below and lateral to the pubic tubercle. What is the most likely diagnosis?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: below and lateral to the pubic tubercle is the femoral canal.
distractorRationale.b: An inguinal hernia lies above and medial to the tubercle.
distractorRationale.c: An umbilical hernia is at the umbilicus, not the groin.
distractorRationale.d: A hydrocele is a scrotal fluid collection and does not have a cough impulse at the femoral canal.

questions.explanation: The pubic tubercle separates the two groin hernias: inguinal above and medial, femoral below and lateral. A femoral hernia carries a higher risk of strangulation because of its narrow neck.

questions.stem: Why are the hernial orifices examined with the patient standing?

options.text: Gravity and raised intra-abdominal pressure make a hernia more visible
The patient can then be examined without consent
Standing relaxes the abdominal wall so hernias disappear
It allows bowel sounds to be heard more clearly

questions.correctOptionText: Gravity and raised intra-abdominal pressure make a hernia more visible

distractorRationale.a: Correct: standing and coughing push the contents through the defect.
distractorRationale.c: Standing makes hernias more, not less, obvious.
distractorRationale.d: Bowel sounds are not the reason for standing.

questions.explanation: Hernias often reduce when the patient lies down, so they can be missed in the supine position. Standing and coughing raise intra-abdominal pressure and let gravity bring the contents into the defect so you can see the cough impulse.

questions.stem: True or false: a bruit heard over the epigastrium proves that the patient has an abdominal aortic aneurysm.
questions.explanation: A bruit shows turbulent flow but does not identify its cause, which could be arterial narrowing, an aneurysm or even a normal variant in a thin patient. It needs to be interpreted with the history, other signs and usually imaging.

questions.stem: Which examination is a recognised component of completing a full abdominal assessment, when indicated and with consent?

options.text: Range of movement of the knee

distractorRationale.a: Correct: it completes the abdominal assessment when indicated.
distractorRationale.b: This belongs to the neurological examination.
distractorRationale.c: Fundoscopy belongs to the eye or neurological examination.
distractorRationale.d: This belongs to the musculoskeletal examination.

questions.explanation: Rectal examination, genital examination, groin nodes, urinalysis and other systems are routine extensions of the abdominal examination. Digital rectal examination must always follow consent and a chaperone offer.

questions.stem: Describe how you would examine the hernial orifices in a 52-year-old man who reports an intermittent groin lump. Include positioning, what you look for and how you distinguish the two main groin hernias.
markingGuide: Introduces self, explains, obtains consent, ensures privacy and offers a chaperone
Examines the patient standing and exposed from umbilicus to mid-thigh
Inspects both groins and scrotum at rest
Asks the patient to cough and looks for a cough impulse
Identifies the pubic tubercle as the landmark
Inguinal hernia is above and medial to the tubercle; femoral hernia is below and lateral
Assesses reducibility and tenderness and does not force an irreducible tender lump
Examines both sides
questions.explanation: A complete answer covers preparation, position, observation with cough, the pubic tubercle landmark and a safe approach to reducibility. The landmark is the key discriminating feature between inguinal and femoral hernias.

questions.stem: A student has finished palpating, percussing and auscultating the abdomen of a 60-year-old man with weight loss and altered bowel habit. List and justify the further examinations that would complete the assessment.
markingGuide: Hernial orifices examined standing with cough
External genitalia examined with consent
Digital rectal examination with consent and chaperone, noting stool colour and blood
Groin nodes and left supraclavicular fossa nodes
Ankle or sacral oedema and other systems as indicated
Urine dipstick and full vital signs
Justification: each step may detect a cause, a complication or a pointer to systemic disease such as malignancy
questions.explanation: The aim is to show that the abdominal examination extends beyond the abdominal wall. With weight loss and altered bowel habit, rectal examination and lymph node examination are especially relevant because they can detect a rectal mass or spread.

questions.stem: Explain why a conclusion that bowel sounds are absent requires a specific approach to listening, and give two clinical conditions in which bowel sounds may be reduced or absent.
markingGuide: Bowel sounds are intermittent
Listen for about two minutes at one site before calling them absent
Warm diaphragm placed lightly on the abdomen
Paralytic (adynamic) ileus as a cause
Generalised peritonitis as a cause
Advanced or late obstruction accepted as a further cause
questions.explanation: Because peristalsis is episodic, a short silence is normal. Only a prolonged silence supports ileus or peritonitis, and it must be interpreted with palpation findings such as guarding.
